units: a neighbour reports that his printing machine was damaging the paper
the user had tried rough handling without getting any result
a local repairer blames the fault on a worn drive belt
the belt had lost its grip through turning with no load
the repairer advises getting at the back of the machine
a round part must be turned one notch to retighten the belt
the machine feeds the paper properly after the intervention
the owner had thought of throwing out a repairable machine
he decides to keep the handbook within reach
text: The chap across the road got talking about his printer, which kept chewing the paper and creasing every sheet it swallowed. He had shaken it, tapped it, tugged at the tray, and got nothing out of it but another jam. Then someone who mends machines round here told him the trouble was almost certainly the drive belt: rubber goes smooth once it has spun for years with nothing to grip. Get round the back, the man said, lift the rear cover, find the grey wheel on the side and turn it one notch to take up the slack. My neighbour grumbled his way through the job. He rang the next morning sounding rather pleased with himself, since the sheets were coming through dead straight at last. He had nearly binned a sound machine over a slack loop of rubber, he said, and the handbook is going in the drawer where he can reach it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of sending messages over distance existed side by side for a long period
the first method used tall towers carrying movable arms
one man set the arms and another read the shape through a glass
the second method sent a current along an insulated metal wire
this wire was buried beside the tracks or hung from supports
mist and darkness stopped the arm system working
the wire worked without depending on the weather
the chain of towers took up a large staff
the electric line kept only one man at each of its ends
the price of the cable held back the spread of the second method
text: Two ways of sending word across country ran alongside each other for a very long stretch of time. One of them raised towers on high ground, each crowned with jointed wooden arms that a man on duty swung into shape, while his opposite number in the next tower read the shape through a glass and repeated it at once. The other pushed a current down a copper wire sheathed in insulation, buried beside the tracks or strung between poles on open ground. Set side by side, the two are not hard to separate. Mist or nightfall stopped the wooden arms dead, whereas the current took no notice of the sky at all. A chain of towers swallowed staff by the dozen, while the wire kept one man busy at either end and nobody in between. What held the wire back was the price of the cable, and that price delayed its spread for a good while.

units: the machine described builds an object by laying matter down in layers
its bulk is comparable to that of a piece of luggage
a reel carries a plastic thread that unwinds towards the machine
a heated tip softens this thread and lays it down in fine ribbons
a moving support drops a little at every pass of the tip
the object is therefore built from the bottom upwards
a fan cools the matter laid down to stop it sagging
an electronic board orders the movements of the whole
the machine is light enough to stand on a household table
text: A machine that lays matter down layer upon layer is housed in a case hardly wider than a suitcase. Look first at the reel, where a translucent plastic filament lies coiled like a patient rope and unwinds without hurry towards the works inside. Then comes the nozzle, a heated tip that softens the thread as it arrives and sets it down in ribbons so fine they feel barely warm to the touch. Under the nozzle the bed slides along, dropping a fraction at every pass the tip makes, so that the object grows as it rises. A fan breathes over the soft trail and sets it firm before it can sag out of shape. Beneath the frame, quiet and out of the way, the board keeps count and orders every movement of the whole. None of it weighs much. The machine stands on an ordinary kitchen table and purrs away like a diligent insect at work.

units: a crew put up a mast on the roof of a technical building
the item installed is a hollow tube made of a light metal
it replaced a device cracked by vibration
the fitters bolted the base onto a thick metal plate
they checked that it stood upright before the final tightening
a rise in the wind set the mast vibrating steadily
the supervisor stopped the work and measured the frequency
the structure was resonating with the gusts
fitting two diagonal stays shifted the natural frequency
the closing measurements confirmed the performance expected
text: Work started before first light, with the crew hauling the mast sections onto the flat roof of the plant room. The aerial itself was a hollow tube of light alloy, brought in to replace one that vibration had cracked through. The fitters bolted the base plate onto a thick steel sheet, then checked that it stood true before pulling the fixings up tight. By midday the wind had freshened and the mast began to hum on one low, steady note. The supervisor called a halt, timed the oscillation and saw what was happening, for the structure was resonating with the gusts. Two diagonal stays went on, which shifted the natural frequency clear of the dangerous band. The cable was terminated as the light went, and the closing measurements confirmed the performance the design had promised.

units: the supply must be cut and the machine left to cool before any work
a hot liquid expands and may be thrown out when the union is opened
a container must be placed beneath the lower union
the draining happens through the weight of the liquid
the valve must be opened a quarter turn only
opening it too quickly draws in air and stops the flow
the bleed control at the high point lets air in at the top
filling is done through the upper opening once the valve is closed
filling slowly keeps bubbles from forming
a circuit without bubbles carries heat evenly
text: Before any work on the cooling circuit, disconnect the supply and leave the machine to cool. Hot water expands, and the pressure it builds inside the flexible hose will throw the liquid out the moment the union is opened. Set a tray beneath the lower union, since the contents drain under their own weight and nothing else. Open the valve a quarter turn and no more. Opened quickly, it draws in air, the flow stalls at once and the whole operation comes to nothing at all. Now lower the bleed lever at the high point, so that air enters at the top and drives the liquid downwards. When the tray stops filling, close the valve, wipe the union and top the circuit up through the upper opening. Filling slowly keeps bubbles from forming, and a circuit free of bubbles carries heat evenly.

units: a voluntary body takes in appliances that no longer work every week
the place used is a covered hall lent by the neighbourhood
most of the objects have a fault of small extent
the faults named are a soldered cell a corroded contact or a glued shell
makers justify these assemblies by waterproofing and slimness
the menders read them as a deliberate shortening of the working life
the workshop records every opening in a register and in pictures
the sheets produced are published for anyone to use
an associated supplier delivers batches of standard contacts
most of the appliances handed in leave in working order
text: In a covered hall lent by the neighbourhood, volunteers take in broken appliances and disheartened owners alike, week after week. Their finding is blunt. Most of what comes through the door has only a small fault: a soldered cell, a corroded contact, a shell glued shut that no ordinary tool will open without breaking it. Makers put these sealed assemblies down to waterproofing and slimness, while the menders read them as a deliberate way of shortening the working life of a product. So the workshop has answered in kind. It keeps a register of every model opened, photographs each stage and publishes the sheets for anyone to use. A parts supplier has joined in and now delivers batches of standard contacts. Since this season, two appliances in three leave the hall working again.

units: two speakers are looked at side by side
the first is a very light plastic cube
its grille imitates the look of metal
the second has a shell of folded metal and weighs more
a stretched cloth covers the front of the second one
the cube lacks power in the low sounds
the heavier one holds the bass notes without shaking
the cube is easy to carry and stands knocks
the second calls for a wall socket and a steady surface
the choice depends on the use intended
text: Stand the two speakers next to each other and the difference shows before you plug anything in. The first is a moulded plastic cube, light as an empty box, with a printed grille that pretends to be metal. The second has weight in the hand: folded sheet metal, edges turned over, and a stretched cloth across the front that hints at a proper cone behind it. Play something and the cube snaps along nicely up top, then gives way as soon as the bass drops. Its heavier neighbour holds the note, fills the room and barely shivers on the shelf. There is the other side of it, mind. The cube slips into a bag, charges overnight and takes knocks without complaint, while the other wants a wall socket and a steady corner. Each has its ground, and the ear decides by what you mean to do with it.

units: the writer disputes the praise given to the thinness of devices
the first charge concerns the battery held on with adhesive
a glued battery condemns the object as soon as its charge fades
the second charge is aimed at screws with an exclusive head
these screws keep independent workshops away from repair
the third charge concerns software that refuses an unpaired part
the three obstacles reinforce one another
the writer grants that shrinking the size forces compromises
he asks that the buyer be told before the purchase
text: We ought to stop praising a device for being thin, as though slimness were a moral achievement. The charge comes under three heads. First the adhesive, since gluing a battery to the frame does the owner no good at all and condemns the thing the moment its charge starts to fade. Then the exclusive screw, cut to a head that no common driver will fit, whose one purpose is to keep the independent workshop out. Last the software, which turns down a spare part identical in every respect because it was not paired at the factory. The three locks work together: the first makes opening risky, the second makes it awkward, the third makes it pointless. Shrinking a device does force compromises, and that much is true. The buyer might at least be told as much at the till, rather than the day after the failure.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a child she took the clocks of her house apart
she rarely put them back together whole
her training took place in a mechanical workshop
that workshop repaired lifting gear
her first job was greasing the grooved wheels
she saw how metal tires and how the grooves wear
once a technician she went down into the pit alone
she carried a hand crank for emergencies at her belt
she was later given the diagnoses her colleagues gave up on
she now passes her trade on to apprentices
text: As a child she took the clocks of the house apart to see what was beating inside them, and rarely got them back together whole. Her training came later, in a mechanical workshop where lifting gear was brought in for repair. Her first job was a dull one, greasing the grooved wheels, one after another, until the cable ran through without a sound. That is where she learned how metal tires and how a groove wears away under the load it carries. Once qualified, she earned the right to go down into the pit alone, a hand crank for emergencies hooked to her belt. In time the awkward diagnoses came to her, the ones her colleagues gave up on. She listens first, palm flat against the upright, and names the guilty part before the housing is even open. She teaches apprentices now, and tells them the ear comes before the tool.

units: the laptop under review weakens as soon as the load runs on
the fault comes from the shape of the machine
a powerful processor sits under a very thin lid
the heat pipe has a reduced cross-section
the heat banks up against the electronic board
the controller drops the clock to protect the chip
the fan grows noisy and the computing speed falls
the keyboard turns warm and long spells of typing suffer
a perforated stand improves the airflow without removing the cause
a thicker chassis would deliver more for the same money
text: This very slim laptop falters as soon as the load runs on for more than a moment, and the reason lies wholly in its shape. A generous processor has been fitted under a lid too thin to leave it room, which gives the heat pipe a laughably small cross-section. With nowhere to go, the heat banks up against the board, and the controller drops the clock at once to keep the silicon safe. You hear the result as much as you measure it: the fan climbs into a whine, computing speed falls by a third, then wanders instead of settling. The keyboard grows warm under the fingers, which tells against any long spell of typing. A perforated stand will improve the airflow and put off the drop, though it treats the effect and leaves the cause alone. For the same money a thicker chassis simply delivers more.
